markdown_report:
The next experiment should test a **recent-item-conditioned GRU readout with BPR-max**, retaining one jointly trained network per category. This remains a hypothesis without demonstrated validation gains.

**Insights from the starting point.** First, supplied scores of 0.4963 and 0.5138 trail the cold start’s 0.5300. These comparisons do not isolate mechanisms, so stronger recency weighting is not justified. Second, Electronics has 22.31% small margins and 9.01% negative-over-positive cases. Competitive-negative training targets this measured weakness, although training margins do not establish ranking quality. Third, users report stale interests and broad matches displacing specific choices. A latest-item-conditioned readout exposes recent evidence while retaining recurrent context; it cannot identify intent directly.

**Insights from related work.** Official GRU4Rec establishes BPR-max, negative-score regularization and larger negative pools [1]. Its sampling differs substantially from the proposed uniform sampler, requiring explicit controls. STAMP and NARM already combine recent evidence with broader session representations [2,3]. They lower the proposal’s originality and motivate tests of whether earlier history contributes. Time-aware GRUs support temporal conditioning, while Ask the GRU supports jointly learned text [4,5]. Neither establishes benefits for this restricted benchmark.

The framework separates three directions: **discrimination** changes objectives and negative pools; **current-interest representation** changes the joint readout; **semantic specificity** adds permitted title/description features.

Scores are originality/potential/user alignment/model alignment/difficulty; higher difficulty means harder implementation.

| Idea | Scores | Benefit; limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Larger-pool BPR-max | 2/7/5/9/4 | Targets competitive errors; weak direct response to stale interests. |
| Recent-item-conditioned readout + BPR-max | 3/6/8/8/5 | Targets recent specificity and margins; risks a transition shortcut. |
| Joint title encoder inside GRU4Rec | 4/7/7/6/7 | May distinguish products; sparse text learning and compatibility inference remain difficult. |

Choose the second idea at 10% progress. Blend each GRU scoring feature with a projected current-item embedding through a learned scalar gate, initialized near zero. This explicitly targets **older interests displacing recent preferences** and **broad affinity displacing specific recent matches**. It does not establish ownership satisfaction or physical compatibility.

Compare baseline, a documented BPR-max control, then its gated counterpart. Hold sampling, initialization of shared parameters, activation, optimizer, reduction and evaluation cadence fixed in the gated comparison. Treat K=128 uniform target-excluding negatives as a separately declared sampling choice; retain explicit score-control comparisons rather than silently equating it with official GRU4Rec.

Select solely by pinned macro validation HR@10. Use affordable, separately trained last-item-only and fixed-gate controls, plus earlier-history perturbations, to investigate shortcut learning. Recheck common sampled margins and twenty-user full-catalog judgments, separating immediate-choice endorsements, stale/broad-interest objections and unidentified content. Preserve every benchmark, diagnostic, routing and single-model constraint.

idea.description: Add a small, jointly trained recent-item residual to the corrected GRU4Rec readout and evaluate it under a controlled BPR-max objective. Each category retains one GRU network and one selected checkpoint. Compare alternative models separately; never combine their predictions.
idea.motivation: The recent-item path explicitly targets two observed user failures: stale interests outranking recent preferences, and broad historical affinity displacing more specific recent matches. BPR-max targets weak sampled discrimination, especially Electronics’ 22.31% small-margin rate and 9.01% negative-over-positive rate. The bypass is a learned item-to-item contribution inside one joint network, so shortcut learning is a central risk. Neither gate values nor aggregate HR establish useful history dependence, intent alignment, complementarity, compatibility or satisfaction.
idea.implementation_notes:
Integration scope: the supplied baseline source is absent, so the code is an integration component rather than a reproducible replacement train.py. Exact baseline architecture, sampler, optimizer, activation, epsilon convention, validation cadence and reduction must be taken from the host-supplied corrected implementation and recorded before execution. Preserve its corrected GRU encoder, embedding scaling/dropout policy, recurrent-state policy and scoring transformation. Apply the residual after the baseline's existing feature transformation, in its scoring dimension. Obtain current-item embeddings through the same documented input transformation used by the encoder; do not accidentally introduce an extra dropout draw. Initialize the scalar gate with zero weights and bias -4, giving approximately 1.8% initial contribution. Initialize the projection using the baseline initialization policy. The initial model is close to, but not exactly, the baseline. Padding features remain zero.

Conceptual limitation: under linear dot-product scoring, the projected latest-item path contributes a learned item-to-item score; a nonlinear output activation changes that algebraic decomposition. This is allowed only as an internal, jointly trained feature path. Do not add separately fitted transition tables, popularity scores or independently fitted experts. STAMP and NARM are relevant precedents for combining recent and contextual representations, although neither is algebraically identical to this scalar-gated bypass. Their session-based results do not demonstrate intent understanding or transfer to long Amazon histories.

Comparison order: retain the corrected baseline as a reference. First compare its objective against BPR-max while holding the actual baseline negative-ID tensors, activation, optimizer and reduction fixed wherever feasible. If moving from a one-negative baseline to a larger pool, explicitly label that comparison as a combined objective/pool intervention; K=1 and lambda=0 provide an algebraic BPR/BPR-max equality check, not an informative hard-negative experiment. Next establish a declared BPR-max control and compare it against the same model with the gated readout, changing only that readout. K=128 total uniform draws per valid transition remains the proposed affordable pool hypothesis, not an official GRU4Rec default. If affordable, compare K=16 and K=128 using prefixes of a fixed maximum-size pool, constant batch size and identical update counts. Do not expand all suggested controls into a full factorial search.

Sampling: for the proposed uniform arm, draw with replacement from real IDs excluding only the current target; padding is never eligible. Retain duplicate IDs and report duplicate rates, unique counts and historical-positive collisions. Skip positions without an eligible negative. Excluding historical positives would define a different sampler and requires a separately identified comparison. No logQ correction is used for BPR-max. Uniform, per-transition, target-excluding sampling changes distribution, sharing and collision handling relative to official GRU4Rec, which combines minibatch targets with shared popularity-tempered additional draws. Its roughly 2,048 additional samples, alpha=0.75 and bpreg=1.0 are reference settings, not validated choices here. Do not attribute a change against that implementation solely to pool size or loss.

Score control: BPR-max includes a separate optional penalty lambda*sum(softmax(negative_scores)*negative_scores^2). It is distinct from optimizer weight decay. Preserve the baseline score activation in controlled comparisons: linear, ELU, ReLU and tanh alter ranges, gradients and softmax concentration. The negative-weight softmax is separate from that activation. Retain the original lambda=0 proposal as an explicitly named arm, and compare lambda=1.0 only if affordable; do not silently transfer the official default across different scoring scales. Select the score-control setting before comparing gated versus ungated readouts, then hold it fixed. Without the penalty, common additive shifts of the scores supplied to BPR-max leave the ranking loss unchanged; scaling still changes margins and negative concentration. This establishes an invariance, not inevitable instability. Monitor score means, norms, extrema and common sampled margins to distinguish score growth from improved ranking.

Loss implementation: gather valid features and targets before scoring. Compute the global negative softmax without detaching weights. Use stable logsumexp for the ranking term. Preserve and record any baseline epsilon convention: -log(exp(C-A)+epsilon) is slightly different from A-C. The supplied function supports either convention. Apply the unchanged baseline position/window/user reduction outside it; never silently replace it with a global position mean. Empty valid batches skip optimization. Keep the same validity masks and negative tensors for the gated comparison.

Memory: dense negative embeddings cost O(N*K*D) for N valid positions and may be expensive even at K=128. If required, checkpoint each chunk's embedding lookup and scoring with torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint(..., use_reentrant=False), passing fixed features and negative IDs explicitly. Concatenate only N-by-K score tensors and compute one global loss, including the global penalty. Alternatively checkpoint chunk logsumexp reductions and merge them with torch.logaddexp; never normalize each chunk separately. Plain Python chunking can retain every chunk's embedding activations until backward and does not establish a reduced training peak. Preserve all scoring parameters and gradients, including any item biases. Measure peak CUDA memory and synchronized full-step runtime, including recomputation; memory feasibility does not establish feasibility within the compute budget.

Controlled randomness: use a dedicated seed-42 sampler stream, separate from model/dropout randomness. Replay or deterministically regenerate identical users, windows and negatives across relevant arms. Initialize shared baseline tensors identically; initialize added modules without changing the shared tensors' initialization draws. Where practical, isolate additional-module randomness so architecture changes do not alter baseline dropout masks. Record any residual stochastic differences rather than claiming fully identical training. Equal update counts do not imply equal GPU time.

Shortcut controls: the minimum decisive training comparison is ungated versus learned-gate GRU4Rec under the same established objective/sampler. If budget permits, separately retrain g=1 latest-item-only and fixed-gate variants; g=0 is the ungated control. A last-item-only variant should omit or bypass unused GRU computation and be identified as a diagnostic comparator, never the submitted replacement for the required GRU backbone. Perturb earlier history while preserving the final item, and compare full versus truncated histories using the same trained model; these are distribution-shift probes, not substitutes for retrained controls. Analyze users sharing a final item and strata defined by training-only transition frequency, history length and item support, reporting sample counts. Gains over a retrained last-item-only comparator and sensitivity to relevant earlier context support, but do not prove, useful conditioning. Gate magnitudes, attention plots and aggregate HR alone cannot establish intent alignment. Stop extending the bypass if its gains concentrate only on frequent transitions or it removes useful earlier-history dependence.

Verification: compare dense and memory-efficient scalar losses and gradients using identical valid masks, parameters and negative IDs. Include features, item embeddings, biases and upstream GRU parameters; use float64 gradcheck on a small deterministic differentiable scorer, repeated IDs, extreme logits and uneven chunks, then verify float32 tolerances. At K=1 and lambda=0, check equality with pairwise BPR. Verify that lambda=0 is invariant to common score shifts at the loss-input level and that the penalty breaks that invariance. Verify g=0 reproduces baseline features, padding remains zero, and training/prediction transformations agree. Test final readout for mixed lengths, singleton and empty rows. Do not infer useful recency from feature sensitivity or diversity from mean embedding alignment.

Protocol: preserve preprocessing seed 0, training seed 42, all four categories Movies_and_TV, Industrial_and_Scientific, Electronics and CDs_and_Vinyl, supplied splits, single-GPU execution, maximum 200 epochs and 200 batches per epoch, and the shared 43,200 GPU-second budget including diagnostics, debugging and failed trials. DATA_DIR remains os.environ['GAGC_DATA_DIR']; write artifacts beneath the trial directory. Respect SASREC_EPOCHS=200 as the host environment default despite the retained variable name. Before execution, record affordable comparison order, maximum updates, baseline validation cadence, checkpoint-selection rule and tie-breaking. Use the host's supplied checkpoint rule; if none exists, prespecify a common evaluation-point rule maximizing macro validation HR@10, breaking ties at the earliest point, and retain one category checkpoint from that selected point. Log all evaluated checkpoints and trials. No optional control is assumed affordable without measured runtime.

Evaluation: select only using unchanged host macro validation HR@10 on 200 users per category and 99 unique negatives with evaluation seed 42. One changed hit changes macro HR by 0.00125. These fixed-candidate results do not establish full-catalog rankings, and repeated validation selection can overfit. Retain all four category results alongside macro HR, report all tried variants, and avoid claims of training-seed robustness from a single required seed. If host-provided paired per-user hit indicators are available, conditional paired uncertainty may be reported with its limited scope; do not invent per-user results or change the evaluator. Hidden tests remain inaccessible and final held-out evaluation remains the host's separate step.

Diagnostics: keep log2feats(sequence) returning aligned B x L features, item_emb, predict_score(features, items), family-specific sample_batch and all ModelView fields. view.model remains the actual trained nn.Module. Preserve DiagnosisProbe(view, device), run_full_diagnosis(train_loader) returning metrics and metric_definitions, and diagnosis_interpreter_prompt(raw_diagnosis). The diagnostic loader remains (None, sequence, positive, negative), each B x L. Existing sampled margins require nonzero input, positive and negative IDs; retain common diagnostic samples across arms independently of optimization pool size. Do not invent item-category breakdowns. Preserve the native full-catalog unseen-item recommendations for twenty real training users, five per category. Track explicit immediate-choice endorsements separately from broad interest, deferred interest, stale-interest objections, functional duplication, compatibility concerns, unestablished tasks and unidentified content. These judgments are descriptive and do not replace the selection metric.

Export: update the embedded predictor writer to instantiate the added projection and gate, load all jointly trained parameters and use identical feature/score transformations. Save architecture configuration, dimensions, activation and empty-history policy. Read the maximum nonpadding position, never count-1, preserving the corrected baseline's handling of empty histories. Export exactly one selected checkpoint per category with all four routes; never average models, checkpoints, scores or ranks. Only public histories, titles, descriptions and timestamps are available, and the selected proposal requires histories only. Do not use unavailable ratings, reviews, item categories, prices, stores, simulator traits, pretrained weights, extra datasets, other trials or their checkpoints.
idea.pseudocode:
import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint


class RecentItemReadout(nn.Module):
    """Attach inside corrected GRU4Rec after its feature transform."""
    def __init__(self, item_dim, feature_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.project = nn.Linear(item_dim, feature_dim, bias=False)
        self.gate = nn.Linear(feature_dim + item_dim, 1)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.gate.weight)
        nn.init.constant_(self.gate.bias, -4.0)
        # Apply the supplied baseline initialization policy to project.
        # Preserve shared baseline initialization when adding this module.

    def forward(self, gru_features, input_embeddings, sequence,
                fixed_gate=None):
        # Features [B,L,D]; transformed input embeddings [B,L,E].
        recent = self.project(input_embeddings)
        if fixed_gate is None:
            gate = torch.sigmoid(self.gate(torch.cat(
                [gru_features, input_embeddings], dim=-1)))
        else:
            gate = float(fixed_gate)  # Diagnostic control; normally None.
        features = (1.0 - gate) * gru_features + gate * recent
        return features.masked_fill(sequence.eq(0).unsqueeze(-1), 0.0)


def bpr_max_position_losses(positive_scores, negative_scores, valid,
                            score_reg=0.0, epsilon=0.0):
    """Return valid-position losses; baseline reduction is external.
    positive_scores [B,L], negative_scores [B,L,K], valid [B,L].
    Inputs already use the baseline scoring activation.
    epsilon must match the declared baseline convention.
    """
    if negative_scores.shape[-1] < 1:
        raise ValueError('At least one eligible negative is required')
    if score_reg < 0 or epsilon < 0:
        raise ValueError('Regularization and epsilon must be nonnegative')
    valid = valid.bool()
    p = positive_scores[valid]
    n = negative_scores[valid]
    # Preserve float64 for gradcheck; promote low precision for stability.
    if p.dtype in (torch.float16, torch.bfloat16):
        p = p.float()
        n = n.float()
    log_weights = F.log_softmax(n, dim=-1)
    log_probability = torch.logsumexp(
        log_weights + F.logsigmoid(p[:, None] - n), dim=-1)
    if epsilon:
        log_epsilon = log_probability.new_tensor(epsilon).log()
        ranking = -torch.logaddexp(log_probability, log_epsilon)
    else:
        ranking = -log_probability
    if score_reg:
        ranking = ranking + score_reg * (
            log_weights.exp() * n.square()).sum(dim=-1)
    return ranking


def checkpointed_negative_scores(features, negative_ids,
                                 score_chunk, chunk_size=16):
    """features [N,D], negative_ids [N,K], after valid gathering.
    score_chunk(features, ids) performs embedding lookup and EXACT
    baseline scoring, including bias/activation, returning [N,C].
    Fixed IDs and a deterministic scorer are required for recomputation.
    All scoring modules must belong to the same trained GRU4Rec.
    """
    if chunk_size < 1 or negative_ids.shape[1] < 1:
        raise ValueError('Positive chunk size and negative count required')
    parts = []
    for ids in negative_ids.split(chunk_size, dim=1):
        parts.append(checkpoint(
            score_chunk, features, ids, use_reentrant=False))
    # Keep only score outputs across chunks; normalize globally afterward.
    return torch.cat(parts, dim=1)


def final_nonpadding_features(features, sequence):
    if sequence.shape[1] == 0:
        return features.new_zeros((sequence.shape[0], features.shape[-1]))
    positions = torch.arange(sequence.shape[1], device=sequence.device)
    last = positions[None, :].expand_as(sequence).masked_fill(
        sequence.eq(0), -1).amax(dim=1)
    result = features[
        torch.arange(sequence.shape[0], device=sequence.device),
        last.clamp_min(0)]
    return result.masked_fill(last.lt(0).unsqueeze(-1), 0.0)


# Integration, using host-supplied baseline components:
# 1. Record actual baseline settings and prespecify affordable comparisons.
# 2. Keep corrected padding-invariant GRU encoding unchanged.
# 3. log2feats(sequence):
#      base, input_embeddings = existing_corrected_encoder(sequence)
#      return recent_readout(base, input_embeddings, sequence)
#    Expose the original baseline branch for the ungated control.
# 4. Gather valid features/targets before negative embedding lookup.
#    Uniform-arm negative IDs exclude zero and current target only.
#    Preserve duplicate columns; keep negative IDs fixed in recomputation.
# 5. Score positives and negatives with identical baseline transformations.
#    Optionally checkpoint negative scoring, then use ONE global softmax.
# 6. Apply BPR-max with declared lambda and epsilon, followed by the
#    unchanged baseline reduction. Skip an empty valid-loss batch.
# 7. Compare gated/ungated arms with matched draws, shared initialization,
#    activation, objective, score penalty, optimizer and update budget.
# 8. Verify dense/checkpointed losses and gradients; measure runtime/memory.
# 9. If affordable, retrain fixed-gate and latest-item-only diagnostic
#    controls; never fuse them or submit them in place of the GRU model.
# 10. Probe earlier-history dependence with the latest item held fixed;
#     report distribution-shift limitations and training-frequency strata.
# 11. Preserve ModelView and diagnostic interfaces and common BxL probes.
# 12. Select only by pinned macro validation HR@10 under the recorded rule.
# 13. Mirror complete architecture/configuration in the predictor writer.
#     Read the maximum nonpadding index and retain empty-history policy.
# 14. Export one selected joint checkpoint per required category, no fusion.

originality.positive: The minimal scalar-gated latest-item bypass provides a focused, diagnosis-motivated adaptation within the required GRU4Rec family.
originality.negative: STAMP, NARM and other session recommenders already combine recent and contextual representations; gated residuals and BPR-max are established, making a score of 4 optimistic.

future_potential.positive: Controlled tests can establish whether exposing latest-item identity adds useful specificity beyond recurrent context before investing in timestamp or text encoders.
future_potential.negative: The bypass may learn frequent item transitions, while sparse validation and a single seed limit evidence; it cannot directly represent compatibility, complementarity or satisfied needs.

code_difficulty.positive: The architecture adds only one projection and scalar gate without additional inference inputs or independently trained components.
code_difficulty.negative: Reproducible sampling controls, global BPR-max regularization, memory-efficient autograd, shortcut diagnostics and predictor-writer consistency require more integration than the small module suggests.

related_work.title: [1] Recurrent Neural Networks with Top-k Gains for Session-based Recommendations
contributions: Establishes BPR-max with softmax-weighted negative competition and a separate negative-score regularization term.
Motivates larger negative pools for competitive ranking.
limitations: Does not establish gains for the proposed gated readout or pinned four-category Amazon evaluation.
Sampler, activation, regularization and reduction choices must be documented rather than treated as interchangeable.

related_work.title: [1] Official GRU4Rec implementation and guidance
contributions: Supports BPR-max and cross-entropy with configurable output activations.
Combines minibatch targets with shared additional samples; documented reference defaults include 2,048 additional samples, popularity exponent 0.75 and bpreg=1.0.
Uses replacement sampling, so duplicate IDs can receive additional aggregate softmax weight.
limitations: The proposed 128 uniform per-transition target-excluding draws differ in count, distribution, sharing and collision handling.
Official defaults and activation guidance do not establish optimal settings under this benchmark.

related_work.title: [2] STAMP author implementation
contributions: Combines latest-item evidence, mean session memory and learned attention.
Uses latest-item conditioning in both attention and multiplicative readout, providing a direct conceptual precedent.
limitations: Its architecture is not the proposed additive scalar-gated GRU bypass.
Session-level results do not establish current-purpose understanding or transfer to Amazon histories.
Original ablation tables were not verified in the supplied evidence.

related_work.title: [3] Neural Attentive Session-based Recommendation
contributions: Combines a final GRU state with attention over earlier GRU states.
Reported hybrid-encoder results support testing complementary contextual representations rather than assuming the latest item is sufficient.
limitations: Its query is the final recurrent state rather than an explicit latest-item-only embedding.
Within-session gains do not demonstrate intent identification or improvements in this constrained setting.

related_work.title: [4] 2Gated-TimeGRU
contributions: Uses interaction intervals in GRU gates to represent changing short-term preferences.
limitations: Motivates temporal conditioning but does not validate the proposed item-conditioned readout.
Timestamp-dependent alternatives require consistent host inference plumbing and cannot assume unknown next-event times.

related_work.title: [5] Ask the GRU: Multi-task Learning for Deep Text Recommendations
contributions: Jointly learns task-specific text representations with collaborative recommendation.
limitations: Its GRU encodes document words rather than interaction histories.
External CBOW embedding initialization does not fit the present restrictions; a randomly initialized text branch remains an unverified adaptation.

related_work.title: PyTorch activation checkpointing documentation
contributions: Documents activation recomputation and the use_reentrant=False checkpoint interface.
Supports checkpointing negative embedding lookup and scoring while retaining global loss normalization.
limitations: Recomputation must use consistent inputs and behavior.
Reduced activation storage does not establish acceptable runtime within the shared GPU budget.

related_work.title: PyTorch gradcheck documentation
contributions: Provides numerical checks of analytical gradients for small double-precision differentiable functions.
limitations: Small gradient checks complement integration tests; they do not establish training quality, inference consistency or benchmark gains.
